# Handling the review report on the front-end technology stack

| Item | Content |
|---|---|
| Original report | `review/metis-review-frontend-stack.md` (GPT, 03/10/2026): conclusion **Can be settled with conditions**; 28 conditions FS-01 to FS-28, of which 12 items "must be fixed before writing the spec", 15 items "should be fixed in Discovery", 1 item "can be considered"; plus 25 missing items in section S9 and a 5-year obsolescence risk table for 33 libraries |
| Applies to | The front-end technical spec, not yet written (this is why the review was run before the spec was written), and the stack decision provisionally settled at the brainstorming session of 03/10/2026 |
| Premises kept unchanged | The output is a real front-end app with sample data, no static prototype, no backend first. The criterion is "best" according to the product owner's nine points. Assumption A-07 stays: the agency has about 40 developers, and scope is not cut because of team size |
| How it was handled | Each claim was checked against the real files before it was accepted. The report read the pack correctly: appendix 14.5 lists exactly the 129 files and 8 directory entries of `metis-frontend-stack-pack.zip`, exactly the 343 lines and 30.222 bytes of `wireframe.css`, and exactly the 7 hard screens that were requested for viewing. No claim about the content of the documents was made up |
| Biggest finding | Three real errors in my proposal, not three differing opinions: (1) the metric cross-check test I proposed **turns green by itself when the formula is wrong**, because four screens call the same function and then assert that they are equal to each other; (2) the gate that compares images with the mid-fidelity wireframe **cannot be right** once the app moves to high fidelity; (3) `wireframe.css` is not CSS to be translated into utility classes but a **component vocabulary** that corresponds one to one with the table in section 6 of the style guide, so Tailwind must sit under a named component layer, not on the markup of the 58 screens |

Result labels: **Accept** (apply the proposal exactly), **Accept with adjustment** (close the same gap another way, with the reason noted), **Needs product owner decision** (touches a decision already settled or involves money), **Rebut** (not applied, with evidence).

Total: 24 Accept, 3 Accept with adjustment, 2 Needs product owner decision (FS-01 and FS-14), 0 Rebut.

## Twelve items that must be fixed before writing the spec

| ID | Proposed content | My verification | Result | Where it goes in the spec |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FS-01** Dense table strategy | Do not rule out AG Grid permanently; run a 10-day acceptance spike comparing TanStack with AG Grid on a 2.000-row fixture and a real screen reader, and only then choose | It is true that the current decision has no execution evidence yet. The report's estimate: 22 to 35 front-end engineer-weeks plus 6 to 10 testing engineer-weeks, about 8 to 12 calendar weeks, for the WBS table alone to reach pilot level. But the report also states that AG Grid is not a sure winner: AG Grid's own documentation says virtualization causes problems for screen readers and recommends turning off virtualization or paginating, while section 17.1 demands 2.000 scrollable items | **Needs product owner decision** | The "open decisions" section of the spec, with the two options in the part further down this file |
| **FS-02** Focus architecture and screen reader labels for the virtualized tree table | Settle before building the grid: a single semantic row in the DOM, pinned columns done with `position: sticky` rather than three separate DOM regions, a focus controller independent of the DOM, `aria-rowcount`, `aria-rowindex`, `aria-level`, `aria-expanded`, and a protocol for entering and leaving edit mode | Correct, and a real gap in my proposal. The traps it names are concrete: the cell that has focus is destroyed by the virtualizer when scrolling, filtering or expanding a branch, so focus falls back to `body`; three separate DOM regions make the screen reader read a row twice. Both are errors I would hit if this were not settled first | **Accept** | A dedicated section on focus architecture, before any description of the table screens |
| **FS-03** Tailwind sits under a named design system | Keep Tailwind but do not let features write strings of utility classes in place of components; tokens stay in `tokens.css`; complex components may use CSS Modules for geometry; each component has a contract ID, a story and a test | Correct. The evidence is `wireframe.css` itself: `.kpi`, `.chip`, `.fresh`, `.save`, `.src`, `.pipeline`, `.board`, `.canvas` are domain vocabulary, not loose styles. This is the way to keep the one-to-one link with section 6 of the style guide while still using Tailwind, which resolves exactly the weakness I had named myself | **Accept** | The UI architecture section, with the three layers of token, theme and component |
| **FS-05** Keyboard parity matrix written before the editor code | Every row has a stable operation ID; write the matrix before coding screens 29 and 58 | Correct. Section 18.4 of the BRD already makes the matrix an output of Discovery, and the second acceptance criterion of `BLD-13` says every row must work in the list editor by keyboard alone. If code comes before the matrix, the two interfaces will form two sets of behavior | **Accept** | The editor section, with the matrix schema |
| **FS-06** The `editor-core` package with a standard command set | Canvas and list must not edit the graph directly; both emit the same set of commands with IDs, typed payloads, preconditions, the record version per `PLT-06`, an idempotency key, domain validation results and audit metadata | Correct, and stronger than my proposal. I said "the graph is our model, canvas and list are two ways to view it", which still lacks the command layer in between. The report's list of 15 commands matches exactly the list of operations that `BLD-13` enumerates. One more benefit: the same command set later becomes the write path of MCP | **Accept** | The editor section, ahead of both canvas screens |
| **FS-09** Separate domain commands from the transport contract | Call the current contract file `provisional.yaml`; commands, errors and the write envelope are hand-written separately per `PLT-06`; generated code exists only in the data access package | Correct. The real risk the report names is not "the API will differ by a few endpoints" but that the front end turns the shape of the interface into the business contract: one endpoint per screen, DTOs mixed with display-only fields, a PATCH that cannot support the expected version, and metrics recomputed by the front end instead of receiving a snapshot from the server | **Accept** | The data contract section |
| **FS-13** Package split | `domain` is split into `domain`, `metrics`, `authz`, `editor-core`; `api-client` is renamed `data-access`; the matrix is contract data, not a runtime package | Correct. These three areas have different owners under the way the 40 people are divided, so package boundaries coincide with ownership boundaries. The point that the matrix must not slip into the product bundle is one I had missed | **Accept with adjustment**: create a package when it gets its first user, do not pre-create all eight empty packages from day one. An empty package is debt, and `nx` adds packages very cheaply | The repo structure section |
| **FS-14** Router and the contract for state in the URL | The 58 screens have no router yet; a typed router must be settled, along with conventions for path parameters and query parameters, and the order of precedence between the URL and a saved view | Correct, and it is an omission of mine, not a matter of opinion. It touches `WBS-20` (a view saves filters, columns, sorting and branch expansion state), `OVW-04` (every metric tile opens the filtered WBS table) and `REG-02` (results update without reloading the page) | **Needs product owner decision** | The navigation section, with two options in the part further down this file |
| **FS-15** Drop the gate that compares images with the wireframe | Replace it with four layers: a per-screen contract, structural comparison, one human side-by-side comparison pass and then signing off a baseline, and only after that use the images of the approved app as the comparison reference | Correct, and this is my error. The wireframe is deliberately mid-fidelity (stated plainly in `wireframes/README.md` line 3), so a high-fidelity app never matches pixel for pixel. The gate I proposed would go red on every correct change | **Accept** | The testing section |
| **FS-17** The metric cross-check test must break when the formula is wrong | Do not let four screens call one function and then assert equality; use a small golden fixture that can be checked by hand, with the expected values stored independently, return a `MetricSnapshot` holding the value, the as-of time and the definition version, and forbid features from importing the function that computes a metric | Correct, and this is the most serious error in my proposal. The test I described is an empty test: if the formula is wrong, all four screens are wrong together and the test stays green. It hits the core of `BR-32`, `BR-39` and the acceptance criteria of `OVW-01` | **Accept** | The metrics section, rewritten entirely |
| **FS-24** Extend the contract of each screen | Add required component IDs and forbidden patterns, data scenarios with an as-of time and a metric version, a list of states, a list of commands, accessibility matrix rows, responsive behavior at three levels, performance budgets, tests per layer, telemetry events, an owner and a reviewer | Correct. `manifest.json` can answer which screen, which area, which requirement, but it cannot stop two people or two agents from choosing different components, different state ownership and a different keyboard model. This is exactly the "generate each screen" part that I am working to settle | **Accept** | The screen generation process section, with the full contract schema |
| **FS-25** Design system governance | Component contract IDs, owners, a deprecation policy, a changelog, and a rule that features must not recreate components with utility classes | Correct, and it is the other side of FS-03: without this rule the semantic layer will be bypassed within a few weeks with 40 people | **Accept** | The UI architecture section |

## Fifteen items that should be done in Discovery

| ID | Content | Verification | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FS-04** Map tokens into Tailwind | Alias only the safe primitive tokens through `@theme inline`; `--focus-ring`, the seven state color groups and the chart color palette stay in components or the semantic adapter | Correct and specific. `--focus-ring` is a two-layer shadow; if a call site sets both another shadow and the focus shadow, the order of the utilities can erase the focus ring, and the focus ring is an accessibility contract. The seven state groups each have three values (dot, text, background); if they are combined separately you get a `critical` background with `waiting` text | **Accept** |
| **FS-07** Diagram layout strategy | ELK only for the hierarchical diagram of screen 27; the two lane screens use a domain coordinate system (lane, day offset, duration); the diagram layout adapter has an asynchronous boundary so it can move to a worker when a threshold is exceeded | Correct. `BLD-03` says a single start date drives the date of every node by offset, so node position has business meaning and must not be decided by a general-purpose layout engine | **Accept** |
| **FS-08** The lifecycle design screen is not a canvas | Keep screen 11 as a structured editor (step list, form, reordering), do not force it into a node-and-edge canvas just to unify the stack | Correct. I re-read `11-lifecycle-framework-designer.html`: its content is a step list, step details, approval gates, criteria and rules, with no canvas. This reduces the number of canvas screens from four to three | **Accept** |
| **FS-10** Code generation tool | Use Orval with several named outputs; a machine runs a check that regenerates and then compares the differences | The direction is right, the tool cannot be verified yet | **Accept with adjustment**: accept the "regenerate and compare differences" gate right away; the choice between Orval and Kubb is left until after a trial session, and is not pinned in the spec while I have not run it |
| **FS-11** Three mock modes | Separate `fixture` (deterministic, nothing saved), `demo` (saves, by named scenario, and can be reset), `contract-test` (simulates record versions, the idempotency key and conflicts faithfully); state clearly which evidence belongs to whom | Correct. The important point: Mock Service Worker running in the browser **does not prove** simultaneous use by several people, tenant isolation or the authorization of MCP. That is exactly the content of appendix B.3 of the BRD | **Accept** |
| **FS-12** Reduce the number of state machines | Keep XState for two jobs: orchestrating saves and conflicts per `PLT-05`, `PLT-06`, and the onboarding flow; the other four lifecycles are typed state-transition tables plus pure guards in the business package | Correct, and my proposal of six machines was overdoing it. The lifecycles of change requests, tenants, workspaces and process frameworks are **stored data** for which the server is the authority; building them as machines running in the browser creates two sources of truth. The UI only needs to ask `canTransition` | **Accept** |
| **FS-16** Requirement coverage graph | The check gate does not only ask "does the requirement have a screen" but asks requirement to screen to state to component to test | Correct, and it matches appendix B.3 of the BRD: a screen coverage figure must never be read as evidence of behavior | **Accept** |
| **FS-18** Deterministic fixtures | A builder of named scenarios, invariants that can be checked, a fixed clock and fixed IDs, contract tests for the fixtures | Correct, and more specific than what I raised. The BRD prints real figures: the CGI Still Renders framework has 16 items and 15 links (`BLD-05`), Nova Energy has 34 projects and 214,6 million EUR. Those figures must become invariants of the fixtures, otherwise the 58 screens will drift away from the documents | **Accept** |
| **FS-19** Accessibility testing | Keyboard tests generated from data, plus one sign-off pass with a real screen reader before the pilot, stored as a versioned artifact | Correct. | **FS-21** Performance | A scenario of 2.000 items, interaction measurement points, a bundle size budget and a long-task budget, trend over time; the threshold for moving ELK to a worker | Correct. Section 17.1 gives 2 seconds at the 95th percentile, but without a repeatable measurement suite that figure cannot be verified | **Accept** |
| **FS-22** Caching policy of the installable app | Pre-cache only static assets with hashes; every API call goes over the network; no writes while offline; clear the cache completely on sign-out and when the tenant changes | Correct, and more important than a mere infrastructure item: `BR-33` says every record belongs to exactly one tenant, so a service worker holding tenant data is an isolation leak path | **Accept** |

## Nine missing items with no ID of their own in the conditions table

Taken from section S9 of the report, the items not yet in FS-01 to FS-28. All are **Accept**.

| What is missing | Consequence if ignored | When it must be decided |
|---|---|---|
| A typed error taxonomy (data validation, permission, session, conflict, transient, severe) with an interface pattern for each kind | Inconsistent messages across the 58 screens; retry, asking for permission and conflict get mixed into one kind | Before the first screen |
| Governance of translation string keys and a simulation of long languages | English and Vietnamese drift apart from each other; the layout breaks when a string is longer | Before the first screen |
| Schema version of saved views, with a migration function and a policy for unknown fields | After columns or filters change, an old view breaks or silently returns wrong results | Before the first saved view of the WBS table and the registry table |
| Order of precedence between the URL and the saved view | The person who receives a shared link sees different results from the sender | At the same time as the router |
| A `Chart` abstraction layer and an equivalent table of numbers for each chart | Each dashboard team picks a different chart library | Before screens 14, 15, 18, 19 |
| Coordination between several browser tabs (session, token, losing canvas write access) | Two tabs editing at once cause confusing conflicts | Before the pilot |
| An audit ledger of dependencies and open source licenses | Legal review comes late, especially with commercial packages or dual licenses | Before the pilot, best before the baseline is locked |
| Policy on source maps and privacy | The product cannot be debugged, or the source code is exposed | Before the pilot |
| Vocabulary of component telemetry events | After the pilot, pain points in saving, tables, filters and the editor cannot be compared | Before the pilot |

One more item with consequences for the backend, taken from section 6.5 of the report: the solution "one person edits one canvas at a time" in section 20 of the BRD is only right if it is a **write-lease contract issued by the server**, with an owner, an acquisition time, an expiry, a keep-alive heartbeat, a read-only viewing mode and a path to request takeover. If it is only a flag in the browser, two tabs still overwrite each other, contrary to `PLT-06`. This is a line that must go into the foundation contract pack in section 18.4 of the BRD, and is not a front-end matter.

## Three places where I adjusted the report's proposal

| Item | What the report says | What I do differently | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| FS-13 package split | Lists eight packages | Create a package when it gets its first user; `domain`, `design-system`, `fixtures`, `contracts` exist right away, `metrics`, `authz`, `editor-core`, `data-access` appear when the first screen needs them | An empty package is maintenance debt, and `nx` adds packages very cheaply. Package boundaries are still declared in advance through import rules, so the rules do not wait for the packages |
| FS-10 code generation tool | Use Orval as the default tool | Accept the regenerate-and-compare gate right away, postpone choosing the tool until after a trial session | I have not run Orval or Kubb on the Metis contract. Pinning a tool in the spec based on its documentation is exactly the kind of claim that pdev requires to be labeled unverified |
| Charts | Choose one chart library before screens 14, 15, 18, 19 | Settle the `Chart` abstraction layer right away, choose the library during the wave of work on those screens | `wireframe.css` already draws `.meter`, `.stackbar`, `.hbars`, `.spark`, `.tl`, `.pipeline` with CSS. Those do not need a library. A library is only needed when a chart appears that CSS cannot draw, and only then will we know what is needed |

## Two decisions needed from the product owner

### Decision one: the dense table, whether to reopen AG Grid (FS-01)

The context has changed since the decision was settled. When "do not buy, build it ourselves" was settled, there was no estimate. Now there is one, and both sides have weaknesses.

The figures to decide with, both of which are estimates and not measurements:

- Building it ourselves on TanStack to pilot level for the WBS table alone: 22 to 35 front-end engineer-weeks plus 6 to 10 testing engineer-weeks, about 8 to 12 calendar weeks with a dedicated squad. Flat tables afterwards are cheaper because the machinery is reused.
- AG Grid Enterprise: listed from USD 999 per developer. The nominal multiplication 40 × 999 is USD 39.960, with volume discounts not yet counted and the terms for the model of an agency building a product to sell to clients not yet confirmed.
- The weakness of AG Grid, taken from its own documentation: virtualization causes problems for screen readers, and the strongest accessibility configuration is to turn off virtualization or use pagination. Section 17.1 of the BRD demands 2.000 items usable within 2 seconds at the 95th percentile, and the wireframe of screen 26 is a scrolling table, not a paginated one.
- The weakness of building it ourselves: all the semantics, the focus model, the keyboard model, the screen reader labels and the in-place editing protocol live in Metis. TanStack only provides state, row handling and the virtualization mechanism.

Two options:

**A. Keep the decision to build it ourselves, run a one-branch architecture spike.** The spike is mandatory because FS-02 needs it: build the right focus controller on the virtualized tree table with pinned columns, a 2.000-row fixture, all 5 levels, in-place editing, filtering that keeps parent rows, two density levels, then verify with a real screen reader. With a stop condition written in advance: if the spike does not meet the keyboard and screen reader matrix at 2.000 rows within the spike budget, only then open the AG Grid branch. Extra cost compared with the current plan: zero, because this spike is needed in every case.

**B. Run a two-branch bake-off right now.** Add an AG Grid branch to the same spike, the same fixture, the same acceptance matrix. Extra cost: about 3 to 4 working days of a small squad plus one trial license. Benefit: if AG Grid passes, dozens of engineer-weeks are bought back.

My proposal is **A**, because it does not touch the decision you already settled, it still requires execution evidence before product code is written, and it keeps the AG Grid door open through a written condition rather than a feeling. Choose **B** if you want to know for certain the figure we are leaving behind.

### Decision two: the router (FS-14)

The 58 screens have no router yet. This is hard to change later because every screen reads its parameters from it.

**TanStack Router.** Query parameters have data types checked at compile time. This is the right feature for Metis, not a convenience: `WBS-20` saves a view made of filters, columns, sorting and branch expansion state; `OVW-04` requires every metric tile to open the filtered WBS table; and the order of precedence between the URL and the saved view is a missing item above. Same family as TanStack Query, Table and Virtual, which we already use. Weakness: younger, smaller community.

**React Router.** More than ten years old, the largest community, almost no obsolescence risk. Weakness: query parameters are strings, so the layer of data types and validation has to be written ourselves with `zod`, and that is exactly the layer most prone to mistakes on the drill-down screens.

My proposal is **TanStack Router**, because the insurance layer for the "few bugs" criterion here comes from the data types of the query parameters, and because the exit cost is low: if a change is needed, the files to edit are the files that define the paths, not the 58 screens, as long as every screen reads parameters through a hook of ours and does not import the router directly. Choose **React Router** if you want to give absolute priority to the criteria of community and stability.

## What does not change after the review

To be clear: the review does not ask to change React, TypeScript, Vite, pnpm, Nx, Tailwind, React Aria, React Flow, TanStack Query, Zod, react-hook-form, i18next, Vitest, Playwright, axe-core, ESLint or Prettier. It also does not ask to go back to a static prototype, does not ask to build the backend first, and does not propose cutting scope. Its conclusion is **can be settled with conditions**, and the conditions lie in how the complex parts are locked down, not in choosing the libraries again.
